intro: Read the deck for the text and these notes for the thinking. The note under each slide explains it, gives you something to remember and warns where people slip. Try each worked example in pencil first. Then close the page and answer the recall questions from memory, using the Article numbers wherever you can.

sections.title: What a Constitution Is & How India's Was Made
sections.big_idea: A constitution is **supreme law** that creates the organs of state, divides power among them and limits what the state may do.
in_plain_words: A constitution confers power and fences it. Parliament, the executive and the judiciary exist because of it, rights bind the state, and a law that conflicts with it is void. For a practitioner, that makes a denied entitlement a legal question as well as an administrative one.

India's was drafted by the Constituent Assembly, which met from December 1946 and debated clause by clause for nearly three years. Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the seven-member Drafting Committee. It was **adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force on 26 January 1950**, and it is the longest written constitution of any sovereign country.

events.what: Government of India Act, last colonial law

diagram.caption: from colonial statute to sovereign republic

key_terms.meaning: The highest law, creating the organs of state and limiting what they may do.
A law inconsistent with the Constitution is invalid and can be struck down.
The body that drafted the Constitution, meeting from December 1946.
The seven-member committee chaired by Ambedkar.
The 1930 pledge of complete independence, honoured in the choice of 26 January.

worked_example.title: Put the dates right
worked_example.setup: A programme leaflet says the Constitution 'came into force on Constitution Day, 1949'. Check it against the deck.
steps: Constitution Day marks adoption by the Assembly on 26 November 1949.
Republic Day marks commencement on 26 January 1950.
The Assembly sat from 1946 to 1949, so 1949 − 1946 = 3 years, which the deck calls nearly three years.
The leaflet confuses the two dates: it should say adopted in 1949 and in force in 1950.
worked_example.answer: Adopted 26 November 1949, in force 26 January 1950, so the leaflet is wrong.

mistakes: Mixing up the adoption date and the commencement date.
Assuming the 1935 Act was discarded. Much of its administrative and federal machinery was kept.
Treating the Constitution as only a political charter. It is law, and conflicting statutes are void.

recall.q: What does supremacy mean in practice?
recall.a: A law inconsistent with the Constitution is invalid and can be struck down.

recall.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee, and how many members did it have?
recall.a: Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired it, and it had seven members.

recall.q: Why was 26 January chosen as the commencement date?
recall.a: It honoured the Purna Swaraj pledge of 1930.

recall.q: How many Schedules were there at adoption, and how many now?
recall.a: Eight at adoption, twelve now.

recall.q: What was the Constituent Assembly Debates used for?
recall.a: It is the primary source for what a provision was meant to do, and courts cite it regularly.

sections.title: The Preamble & Its Values
sections.big_idea: The Preamble puts sovereignty in the people and states the goals of **justice, liberty, equality and fraternity**, yet it is a guide and no source of power.
in_plain_words: 'We, the People of India' locates sovereignty in the people. The Preamble calls India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic. Socialist and Secular were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, and the 44th Amendment retained them. Courts hold that secularism was implicit from the start.

The Preamble grants no powers and you cannot sue on it alone, but courts use it to read ambiguous provisions, and it is part of the Constitution. Ambedkar called fraternity the keystone. Indian secularism is **principled distance**: no state religion, equal treatment of all faiths, and room to reform religious practice for equality.

right.title: The Preamble is not
items: A basis for a suit on its own

diagram.caption: what it can and cannot do in court

key_terms.meaning: Ultimate authority belongs to the people, who give themselves the Constitution.
Assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity of the nation.
A state with no religion that may intervene to secure equality.
Added Socialist and Secular to the Preamble in 1976.
A text courts use to read an ambiguous provision.

worked_example.title: Test a policy against the Preamble
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A state scheme gives ration cards only to families with a permanent address. Apply the four Preamble questions.
steps: Justice: does it reach those worst off? Migrants and the homeless may be excluded.
Liberty: does it constrain anyone unnecessarily? It ties families to one place.
Equality: of status, or only of opportunity? Families without an address lose status as well.
Fraternity: does it strengthen or divide? It splits residents from newcomers.
worked_example.answer: The scheme fails the four-question test, which gives you an argument but no right to sue on the Preamble alone.

mistakes: Saying the Preamble gives enforceable rights. It does not.
Believing Socialist and Secular were in the 1949 text. They arrived in 1976.
Reading Indian secularism as a strict wall between religion and state.

recall.q: When were Socialist and Secular added?
recall.a: By the 42nd Amendment in 1976, and retained by the 44th Amendment in 1978.

recall.q: What did Kesavananda Bharati hold about the Preamble?
recall.a: It is part of the Constitution and can be amended, subject to the basic-structure limit.

recall.q: Which four goals does the Preamble name?
recall.a: Justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

recall.q: Why did Ambedkar single out fraternity?
recall.a: Without it, liberty and equality could not be sustained in a society scarred by caste.

recall.q: What is principled distance?
recall.a: The state has no religion, treats all faiths equally, and may intervene to reform practices in the name of rights and equality.

sections.title: Fundamental Rights I: Equality & Freedoms
sections.big_idea: Part III rights are **enforceable against the state**, and knowing the Article for your issue changes what you can argue.
in_plain_words: Part III (Articles 12 to 35) guarantees rights that courts can enforce, with a direct route to the Supreme Court under Article 32. Most bind the state, with exceptions that reach private persons: Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24. Article 14 allows reasonable classification, which is why reservation fits within equality.

Article 19 lists six freedoms, each subject to reasonable restrictions on listed grounds. Articles 20 to 22 protect liberty and arrest safeguards. Article 21 has grown to cover dignity, livelihood, privacy and a clean environment. **Article 21 is the workhorse of public-interest litigation.**

diagram.caption: equality and freedoms in one view

key_terms.meaning: Justiciable rights in Part III, Articles 12 to 35.
A distinction based on an intelligible differentia with a rational aim.
Abolishes untouchability and binds private persons as well as the state.
Life and personal liberty, read by courts to include dignity and privacy.
A limit on a freedom that must fall within the grounds listed in the clause.

worked_example.title: Find the handle
worked_example.setup: Match each field situation to the Article that gives it constitutional weight.
steps: Rations or wages denied: Article 21, the right to livelihood.
Caste exclusion from a public place: Articles 15(2) and 17.
Arbitrary detention of a poor person: Articles 21 and 22, including production before a magistrate within twenty-four hours.
A union's registration refused: Article 19, freedom to form associations.

mistakes: Reading Article 14 as a ban on all differential treatment. Reasonable classification is allowed.
Assuming every Fundamental Right can be used against a private person. Only a few can.
Treating Article 19 freedoms as absolute. They carry reasonable restrictions.

recall.q: Which Articles cover the Right to Equality?
recall.a: Articles 14 to 18.

recall.q: What are the two parts of the test for a classification under Article 14?
recall.a: An intelligible differentia, and a rational relation between that differentia and the law's object.

recall.q: What are the enabling provisions for affirmative action?
recall.a: Articles 15(3) and 16(4), which enable it without making it mandatory.

recall.q: What does Article 22 require within twenty-four hours?
recall.a: An arrested person must be produced before a magistrate, excluding travel time.

recall.q: Which case held that a procedure depriving liberty must be fair, just and reasonable?
recall.a: Maneka Gandhi (1978).

sections.title: Fundamental Rights II: Protection, Remedies
sections.big_idea: A right without a remedy is hollow, so **Article 32 and Article 226** are the doors through which every other right is enforced.
in_plain_words: Article 23 bars trafficking and forced labour, and Article 24 bars hazardous work by children under 14. Articles 25 to 28 protect freedom of religion, and Articles 29 and 30 protect minority language, culture and institutions. Article 25 is subject to public order, morality and health, which is how reform laws can override a practice.

Article 32 lets any person go directly to the Supreme Court for Part III rights. Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ power, so it is often the more practical route. Five writs are available. **Mandamus matters most in development work**, because it compels an authority to perform a legal duty.

key_terms.meaning: 'Produce the body': a challenge to unlawful detention.
'We command': an order to an authority to do its legal duty.
A writ quashing an order passed without jurisdiction or in error.
Forced labour without pay, barred by Article 23.
A court test of which religious practices attract protection.

worked_example.title: Choose the writ
worked_example.setup: Pick the writ for each situation.
steps: A woman is held with no order: habeas corpus.
A department refuses to release a sanctioned pension: mandamus.
A lower court takes up a case outside its jurisdiction: prohibition.
A person holds a public office without legal authority: quo warranto.
worked_example.answer: Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition and quo warranto, with certiorari for quashing an order already passed.

mistakes: Going to the Supreme Court for a non-Fundamental right. Article 226 covers any legal right.
Filing a writ before trying administrative remedies where the duty is unclear.
Treating Article 29 as only for minorities. It protects any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture.

recall.q: What did Ambedkar call Article 32?
recall.a: The very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it.

recall.q: What is the difference between Article 32 and Article 226?
recall.a: Article 32 covers Fundamental Rights, while Article 226 covers those and any other legal right.

recall.q: What did the 44th Amendment protect during a national emergency?
recall.a: Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.

recall.q: Which Article bars begar and forced labour?
recall.a: Article 23.

recall.q: Who may establish and administer educational institutions of their choice under Article 30?
recall.a: Religious and linguistic minorities.

sections.title: Directive Principles & Fundamental Duties
sections.big_idea: Directive Principles are a **road for the state** and Fundamental Rights a wall, yet courts have turned many directives into enforceable rights.
in_plain_words: Part IV (Articles 36 to 51) sets goals such as livelihood, equal pay, free legal aid and panchayats. Under Article 37 they cannot be enforced by a court, and they remain fundamental in governance. They have shaped statutes and rights, and courts use them to interpret Fundamental Rights.

The pattern is that a directive sits unenforced for decades and then becomes a statute or is read into Article 21. **Education is the clearest case**. Fundamental Duties in Article 51A, added in 1976, address citizens. They too cannot be enforced directly, and courts have refused to use them to cut down rights.

diagram.caption: how a directive became a right

key_terms.meaning: Not directly enforceable in court.
Goals in Part IV that direct the state toward social and economic justice.
Reading rights and directives together without setting them against each other.
Created in 1951 to shield land-reform laws from challenge.
Citizens' obligations in Article 51A, added in 1976.

worked_example.title: Trace a directive
worked_example.setup: Follow the education directive from Part IV to a statute, as the deck does.
steps: The directive says the state should provide for education.
Courts read education into the right to life under Article 21.
The 86th Amendment makes it explicit as Article 21A in 2002.
The Right to Education Act follows in 2009, so 2009 − 2002 = 7 years later.
worked_example.answer: A directive became a right in 2002 and a statute seven years after that.

mistakes: Calling Directive Principles irrelevant because they are non-justiciable. Courts use them to read rights.
Using a Fundamental Duty to cut down a right. Courts have resisted it.
Forgetting that duties are addressed to citizens, while rights and directives address the state.

recall.q: What does Article 37 say about the Directive Principles?
recall.a: They are not enforceable by any court, yet they are fundamental in the governance of the country.

recall.q: Which Article covers free legal aid?
recall.a: Article 39A, added by the 42nd Amendment.

recall.q: How many Fundamental Duties were there originally, and how many now?
recall.a: Ten originally, with an eleventh added in 2002.

recall.q: Which amendment created the Ninth Schedule?
recall.a: The First Amendment, in 1951.

recall.q: What is the settled position on rights and directives?
recall.a: The state should harmonise the two and may pursue directives without destroying the basic structure.

sections.title: The Union Government & Its Structure
sections.big_idea: India has a **parliamentary** system in which the real executive comes from, and answers to, the legislature, while the courts carry the structural checks.
in_plain_words: The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers are drawn from Parliament and must hold the confidence of the Lok Sabha. The President is head of state and acts on ministerial advice. Parliament has two Houses: the directly elected Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha, which represents the states and is permanent.

A Bill must pass both Houses and receive assent, and a Money Bill favours the Lok Sabha. The separation of powers is functional and flexible, because the executive sits inside the legislature. **That places the structural load on judicial review.** Figures for House strength on the slide are approximate maxima.

right.title: Rajya Sabha
items: Permanent, one-third retire every two years
May only recommend on Money Bills

key_terms.meaning: The real executive, collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
A Bill the Rajya Sabha may only recommend changes to.
A way to resolve a deadlock on an ordinary Bill.
Organs have distinct roles, though the executive sits in the legislature.
The Council answers to the House together.

worked_example.title: Turnover in the Rajya Sabha
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. The deck gives around 250 as the approximate maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha, and one-third of members retire every two years.
steps: Members retiring each time: 250 ÷ 3 = 83.
Because the House is permanent, about two-thirds stay, so it is never fully dissolved.
The Lok Sabha, by contrast, can be dissolved after five years.
worked_example.answer: About 83 members retire every two years, and the House itself continues.

mistakes: Treating the President as the real executive. The President acts on advice.
Assuming the Rajya Sabha can bring down a government or block a Money Bill. It cannot.
Reading the strength figures as current. They are approximate maxima.

recall.q: What does Article 74 require of the President?
recall.a: The President must act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.

recall.q: Which House decides who governs?
recall.a: The Lok Sabha, whose confidence the government must hold.

recall.q: What can a joint sitting resolve, and what can it not?
recall.a: A deadlock on an ordinary Bill, and it is unavailable for Constitutional Amendment Bills.

recall.q: Who is ex-officio Chairperson of the Rajya Sabha?
recall.a: The Vice-President.

recall.q: Why is the Money Bill classification contested?
recall.a: The Rajya Sabha cannot block a Money Bill, and the Speaker's certification decides the classification.

sections.title: Federalism: Union, States & the Schedules
sections.big_idea: India is a federation with a **strong Centre**, built to hold a diverse nation together, and the Seventh Schedule tells you who owes the duty.
in_plain_words: The Seventh Schedule has three lists. Parliament alone legislates on the Union List, state legislatures on the State List, and both on the Concurrent List, where Union law generally prevails. Residuary powers rest with the Union under Article 248. Education and forests moved to the Concurrent List in 1976.

Centralising features include President's Rule under Article 356, a Governor appointed by the Centre and Parliament's power over boundaries. S.R. Bommai (1994) made Article 356 reviewable. In practice governance is cooperative, through the Finance Commission and GST Council, and **asymmetric**, with the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for tribal areas.

key_terms.meaning: Power over subjects on no list, held by Parliament under Article 248.
Union takeover of a state's executive powers under Article 356.
A federation formed to hold diversity in a union, with a tilt to the Centre.
A shared body for indirect tax rates and design.
Tribal areas under the Fifth Schedule.

worked_example.title: Which level owes the duty?
worked_example.setup: Use the Seventh Schedule to place four subjects.
steps: Railways: Union List, so Parliament alone legislates.
Police: State List, so the state legislature legislates.
Education: Concurrent List since 1976, so both legislate and the Union law prevails in a clash.
A subject on no list: residuary, so Parliament under Article 248.
worked_example.answer: Union, State, Concurrent and Union again, and the answer tells you which government to approach.

mistakes: Looking to the state for a Union List subject, or the Centre for a State List one.
Forgetting that education and forests moved to the Concurrent List in 1976.
Describing Article 356 as unreviewable. Bommai made it reviewable and required a floor test.

recall.q: Which Article gives residuary powers to the Union?
recall.a: Article 248.

recall.q: What did Bommai hold?
recall.a: Article 356 is reviewable, a floor test is required, and federalism and secularism are part of the basic structure.

recall.q: Name the three kinds of emergency and their Articles.
recall.a: National emergency (352), President's Rule (356), financial emergency (360).

recall.q: How often has a financial emergency been proclaimed?
recall.a: Never.

recall.q: Which Schedules cover tribal areas?
recall.a: The Fifth Schedule for Scheduled Areas and the Sixth for tribal areas in the North East.

sections.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
sections.big_idea: One integrated court system applies both Union and state law, and **judicial review** is how the Constitution's supremacy is enforced.
in_plain_words: The Supreme Court sits at the apex, High Courts in the states and subordinate courts below. Independence rests on secure tenure, salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund and a hard removal process. The collegium is a judicial creation, and the NJAC was struck down in 2015.

Judicial review lets courts strike down unconstitutional laws and quash executive action, though not legislate or amend. Public Interest Litigation relaxed standing so third parties can act for the marginalised. **Kesavananda Bharati (1973) is the pivot**: Parliament may amend but not destroy the basic structure.

diagram.caption: one ladder applying Union and state law

key_terms.meaning: The judicially evolved system for appointing higher judges.
The power to declare laws and executive acts void if they violate the Constitution.
Public Interest Litigation, which relaxed who may sue.
A case kept open for years with interim orders and monitoring.
Core features that no amendment can destroy.

worked_example.title: Pick the forum
worked_example.setup: A department has refused to release a sanctioned entitlement to a village.
steps: Check that administrative remedies were tried and the duty is clear.
The right is a legal one and may fall outside Part III, so Article 226 at the High Court fits.
Article 32 at the Supreme Court is open only for Part III rights.
The remedy sought is mandamus, to compel the authority to perform its legal duty.
worked_example.answer: A mandamus petition in the High Court under Article 226 is the practical first route.

mistakes: Treating judicial review as a power over policy in detail. The slide lists that as beyond it.
Calling the collegium a constitutional provision. It is a judicial creation.
Underrating Kesavananda. A 13-judge bench, the largest ever, decided it by a narrow majority.

recall.q: Which jurisdictions does the Supreme Court have?
recall.a: Original, appellate, advisory under Article 143, and special leave under Article 136.

recall.q: What did Kesavananda Bharati hold?
recall.a: Parliament can amend any provision but cannot destroy the basic structure.

recall.q: Name three features recognised as basic structure.
recall.a: Any three of: supremacy of the Constitution, judicial review, separation of powers, federalism, secularism, free and fair elections.

recall.q: What did Minerva Mills hold?
recall.a: Limited amending power is itself part of the basic structure.

recall.q: How is PIL criticised?
recall.a: For judicial overreach, elite capture of the docket, and orders that are hard to implement.

sections.title: Local Self-Government
sections.big_idea: The 73rd and 74th Amendments made local government **a constitutional mandate**, and left real power to be devolved by the states.
in_plain_words: The 73rd Amendment added Part IX for panchayats and the 74th added Part IX-A for municipalities, both in force in 1993. They require elections every five years through a State Election Commission, reserved seats for SC, ST and women, and a State Finance Commission. Panchayats have three tiers: village, block and district.

The Gram Sabha is the assembly of all adult voters, a rare face-to-face democratic body. Power on paper differs from power in practice, and the three Fs of **funds, functions and functionaries** must come together. PESA gives Gram Sabhas in Scheduled Areas stronger powers over land and forest produce.

diagram.caption: the three panchayat tiers, each elected

key_terms.meaning: The assembly of all adult voters of a village.
Constitutionalised panchayats through Part IX.
Constitutionalised municipalities through Part IX-A.
Funds, functions and functionaries, the three things devolution needs.
The 1996 Act extending Part IX to Fifth Schedule areas with stronger Gram Sabha powers.

worked_example.title: Count reserved seats
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A panchayat has 30 seats. SC and ST together make up 20 per cent of its population, and the state reserves one-third of seats for women.
steps: SC and ST seats in proportion to population: 30 × 20 ÷ 100 = 6.
Women's seats at the constitutional floor of one-third: 30 ÷ 3 = 10.
If the state raised the share to one-half, as many states have: 30 ÷ 2 = 15.
worked_example.answer: Six SC and ST seats, at least ten seats for women, and fifteen if the state reserves one-half.

mistakes: Assuming a panchayat decides everything the Eleventh Schedule lists. The Schedule lists subjects states may devolve.
Counting one-half women's reservation as a constitutional requirement. It is state legislation.
Treating the Gram Sabha as active everywhere. Quorum failure and domination by the same interests are common.

recall.q: Which Parts did the 73rd and 74th Amendments add?
recall.a: Part IX for panchayats and Part IX-A for municipalities.

recall.q: What are the three Fs?
recall.a: Funds, functions and functionaries.

recall.q: How many functions does the Eleventh Schedule list?
What is the constitutional minimum reservation for women?
recall.a: At least one-third of seats.

recall.q: Name two powers PESA gives the Gram Sabha in Scheduled Areas.
recall.a: A say over land acquisition, and control of minor forest produce.

sections.title: Amending the Constitution
sections.big_idea: The Constitution is a living document with **three amendment routes**, and a protected core that no majority can amend away.
in_plain_words: Article 368 sets Parliament's power to amend, and the bar rises with the depth of the change. Some provisions need only a simple majority outside Article 368. Most need a special majority. Federal provisions also need ratification by half the state legislatures.

Landmark amendments include the 42nd (1976), the 44th (1978), the 73rd and 74th (1992), the 86th (2002) and the 101st (2016). The courts added the limit: Golaknath, then Kesavananda and Minerva Mills. The Constitution evolves by amendment and by interpretation, and **interpretation leaves no trace in the text**.

diagram.caption: the deeper the change, the higher the bar

key_terms.meaning: The clause setting Parliament's amending power and procedure.
A majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting.
Approval by half the state legislatures for federal provisions.
The 1967 case saying rights could not be amended, later overruled.
Placing some rules beyond the reach of a temporary majority.

worked_example.title: Count a special majority
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A House has 500 members in total and 400 are present and voting. A special majority needs both a majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting.
steps: Majority of total membership: 500 ÷ 2 = 250, so at least 251 votes.
Two-thirds of those present and voting: 400 × 2 ÷ 3 = 267.
Both conditions must hold at once, so the binding figure is 267 votes.
For a federal provision, half the state legislatures must also ratify.
worked_example.answer: At least 267 votes in this illustration, plus ratification by half the states if the change is federal.

mistakes: Treating every amendment as needing the states. Only federal provisions do.
Thinking the protected core is in the text. It came from the courts in Kesavananda.
Reading the amendments-per-decade chart as exact. It is illustrative.

recall.q: What majority is required for a special-majority amendment?
recall.a: A majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting in each House.

recall.q: Which amendment introduced the GST?
recall.a: The 101st, in 2016.

recall.q: What did the 44th Amendment do to the right to property?
recall.a: It removed it from Part III and made it a constitutional right under Article 300A.

recall.q: Name the cases in the sequence on the amending power.
recall.a: Golaknath (1967), the 24th and 25th Amendments, Kesavananda (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980).

recall.q: In what two ways does the Constitution evolve?
recall.a: By amendment, which is visible, and by interpretation, which leaves no trace in the text.

sections.title: Constitutionalism in Practice
sections.big_idea: Having a constitution is a start, and **constitutionalism** means its restraints are observed, which you can check in courts, elections and rights.
in_plain_words: Constitutionalism is limiting government in practice: independent courts, free elections and a rights culture. Many states have fine texts and no constitutionalism. A rights-based approach turns beneficiaries into rights-holders with the state as duty-bearer, and changes what a programme builds, demands and audits.

Landmark laws trace back to constitutional roots, such as RTE to Article 21A and RTI to Article 19(1)(a). Puttaswamy (2017) found privacy within Article 21, and NALSA and Navtej Johar built on dignity and equality. **Naming the constitutional basis turns a request into a claim.**

diagram.caption: each landmark law has a constitutional root

key_terms.meaning: Actually limiting government by constitutional rules.
A person with constitutional and legal entitlements, owed by a duty-bearer.
The right to demand records from public authorities, with a deadline.
The test of legality, necessity and proportionality from Puttaswamy.
Knowing the Article behind an entitlement, which transfers to others.

worked_example.title: Sharpen an RTI request
worked_example.setup: A pension was stopped and a worker asks the office, 'Why was my pension stopped?'
steps: A question can be refused, but a request for a specific file usually cannot.
Rewrite it: ask for the file noting and the order that stopped the pension.
Cite Article 19(1)(a) and the RTI Act, and note the thirty-day deadline.
If refused, appeal first, then go to the Information Commission.
worked_example.answer: Ask for the file and the order, with the deadline and appeal path in mind.

mistakes: Treating RTI as a way to ask for explanations. Ask for documents.
Assuming a good constitutional text guarantees constitutionalism.
Forgetting that the constitutional provision stays available even if a statute's own remedy is blocked.

recall.q: What is the difference between having a constitution and constitutionalism?
recall.a: A constitution is a document, while constitutionalism means its restraints are actually observed.

recall.q: What is the usual deadline for an RTI reply?
recall.a: Thirty days, generally.

recall.q: What did Puttaswamy hold?
recall.a: Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21, decided by a nine-judge bench.

recall.q: What is the constitutional basis for voting?
recall.a: Article 326, universal adult suffrage.

recall.q: Which takeaway does the deck say to keep if you keep one?
recall.a: Power is divided, so ask which level owes the duty.

notes.2: Use the agenda as the course map. Sections one and two cover why constitutions exist and what the Preamble promises, three to five cover rights, principles and duties, and six to nine cover how government is built. Ten and eleven show how the text changes and how it is used in practice.
notes.4: Start with supremacy. A constitution creates the organs of state, divides power among them and limits what the state may do, and a conflicting statute is void. For a practitioner this means a denied entitlement may be a legal question as well as an administrative one.
notes.5: Remember the two jobs as a pair: the Constitution confers power and it limits power. A government defending an action argues from the first column and a citizen challenging it argues from the second. Both read the same text, so name which job a provision does before you argue from it.
notes.6: Read the table as four reversals of colonial rule: authority from the people, universal adult suffrage, justiciable rights, and an executive answerable to Parliament. Much of the 1935 Act's machinery was kept, which explains why the Constitution is long and why its structure feels familiar in places.
notes.7: The Constituent Assembly debated clause by clause in the open for nearly three years, from December 1946. Its published Debates are the primary source for what a provision was meant to do, and courts cite them regularly. Reading the debate on a provision you work with is worth an hour.
notes.8: Note Ambedkar's two roles: chair of the seven-member Drafting Committee, and the person who defended the draft clause by clause. The quotation matters for practice, since it says a constitution is only as good as those who work it. His closing speech on political and social democracy is worth reading in full.
notes.9: Get the two dates the right way round: adoption on 26 November 1949, now Constitution Day, and commencement on 26 January 1950, Republic Day. The gap was deliberate, because 26 January had marked Purna Swaraj since 1930. Programme materials often confuse the two.
notes.10: The Constitution is the longest written constitution of any sovereign country, with around 395 Articles and eight Schedules at adoption, now twelve. Length was a deliberate choice, since detailed provisions constrain a new administration. Letters in numbering, such as 21A, explain why the count of provisions exceeds the highest number.
notes.12: Notice where the Preamble puts sovereignty: in the people, and in no Crown. That was a substantive claim in 1949. Also remember that Socialist and Secular were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, so the Preamble as adopted did not contain them.
notes.13: Popular sovereignty means authority comes from the governed, who gave the Constitution to themselves. The phrase does legal work, because it settles where validity comes from: the Constituent Assembly acting for the people, and the Indian Independence Act plays no such role. Use the table to contrast it with a Crown or a founder.
notes.14: Learn the five words as a set, and memorise which two arrived late. Socialist and Secular were added in 1976 and retained by the 44th Amendment in 1978. Courts have held that secularism was implicit in the original text and is part of the basic structure, so the values were present from the start.
notes.15: Use the four goals as a vocabulary: justice (social, economic and political), liberty, equality and fraternity. Justice lists social and economic before political, which supports reading the Constitution as a document of social transformation. The ideals were reworked for India's struggle against caste, colonialism and inequality.
notes.16: Fraternity is the keystone because Ambedkar argued that liberty and equality could not hold without it in a society scarred by caste. One person, one vote is a start, and the goal is one person, one value. His warning that the Constitution works only as well as its operators returns in Section 11.
notes.17: Separate three ideas. The Preamble grants no powers and creates no enforceable rights, so you cannot sue on it alone. Courts use it to interpret ambiguous provisions. And it is part of the Constitution, amendable only within the basic-structure limit, as Kesavananda Bharati held.
notes.18: Indian secularism is principled distance. The state has no religion, treats all faiths equally, and may intervene to reform religious practice for rights and equality, such as abolishing untouchability. That engagement separates the Indian model from the American one and is the source of most live controversy.
notes.19: Treat the Preamble as a four-question test for any policy: does it reach those worst off, does it constrain anyone unnecessarily, does it give equality of status or only of opportunity, and does it strengthen or divide? It is a standard to argue from, though it creates no enforceable right.
notes.21: Fundamental Rights are justiciable, so a person can go to court when they are infringed, and Article 32 gives a direct route to the Supreme Court. Most are held against the state and are subject to reasonable restriction. Remember the exceptions that reach private persons: Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24.
notes.22: Use the table to find the Article for your issue, because that changes what you can argue. Six families run from equality (14 to 18) to remedies (32). The right to property is the one that left Part III, removed by the 44th Amendment in 1978 and now found in Article 300A.
notes.23: Article 14 permits reasonable classification and forbids arbitrary distinction. The courts ask two questions: is there an intelligible differentia, and does it relate rationally to the law's object? That test is why reservation and targeted schemes fit with equality, since unequal treatment with a rational basis is what the Article contemplates.
notes.24: Articles 15 and 16 are the constitutional basis for affirmative action, and they enable it without making it mandatory. Article 15 bars discrimination on grounds including caste and sex and permits special provision. Article 16 covers public employment. Later clauses were added by amendment, each responding to a judicial decision.
notes.25: Article 17 is unusual because it abolishes untouchability outright, binds private persons and requires punishment by law. Learn the chain for caste exclusion in a village: Article 17, then the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 and the SC/ST Atrocities Act 1989, then the special court. Article 18 abolishes titles.
notes.26: Memorise the six freedoms of Article 19, then the rule that each is subject to reasonable restrictions on listed grounds. A restriction outside those grounds is invalid, and courts decide whether it is reasonable. The right to form associations is the basis for unions and registered organisations.
notes.27: Articles 20 to 22 protect liberty. Article 20 guards against arbitrary conviction, 21 covers life and personal liberty, 21A gives education from 6 to 14, and 22 sets safeguards on arrest. Remember the detail for detention work: an arrested person must be produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours, excluding travel time.
notes.28: Follow Article 21's growth in the table: fair, just and reasonable procedure in Maneka Gandhi (1978), livelihood in Olga Tellis (1985) and privacy in Puttaswamy (2017). Courts read dignity into 'life', which is why Article 21 is the workhorse of public-interest litigation on health, shelter, food and environment.
notes.30: Article 23 bars trafficking, begar and forced labour, and Article 24 bars hazardous work by children under 14. Courts have held that work paid below the minimum wage can amount to forced labour. That reading helps in the field, since compelled unpaid work is a constitutional violation as well as a labour-law breach.
notes.31: Article 25 is the core freedom of religion, and it is expressly subject to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III, which allows reform legislation to override a practice. The essential-practices test decides which practices are protected, and it is contested yet decisive in practice.
notes.32: Compare Articles 29 and 30 closely. Article 29 protects any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture, and Article 30 is expressly a minority right to establish and run educational institutions. The distinction matters in litigation, and Article 30 is among the most litigated provisions in education.
notes.33: Article 32 makes every other right real, because a right without a remedy is hollow. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution. Remember its limit: it covers Part III rights only. Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ power, so it is often the more practical route.
notes.34: Match each writ to a situation: habeas corpus for unlawful detention, mandamus to compel a legal duty, prohibition against a lower court exceeding jurisdiction, certiorari to quash an order, and quo warranto against an unlawful office-holder. Mandamus matters most in development work, for example to release a sanctioned entitlement.
notes.35: Rights are strong and have limits. They can be reasonably restricted and suspended in a national emergency, but after 1975 to 1977 the 44th Amendment protected Articles 20 and 21 from suspension and tightened the trigger to armed rebellion. A law authorising a restriction is not enough; the restriction must be fair and proportionate.
notes.36: Use the table as a field lookup from situation to Article. Rations or wages denied point to Article 21, caste exclusion to Articles 15(2) and 17, arbitrary detention to 21 and 22, bonded labour to 23, and child labour to 24. Knowing the Article turns a request into a claim and tells you the remedy route.
notes.38: Directive Principles in Part IV (Articles 36 to 51) set goals for the state and cannot be enforced in court by themselves. Learn a few Articles: 38 social order, 39 livelihood and equal pay, 39A free legal aid, 40 panchayats, 43 living wage. Article 39A is the basis of legal services authorities.
notes.39: Hold Ambedkar's picture: Fundamental Rights are a wall the state cannot cross, and Directive Principles are a road it should travel. Article 37 says they are unenforceable by courts and still fundamental in governance. Non-justiciable does not mean irrelevant, since courts use them to interpret rights.
notes.40: Notice the pattern in the table: a directive sits unenforced for decades and then becomes a statute or is read into Article 21. Education, panchayats and food security show it. For an advocate, an unimplemented Directive Principle is a legitimate argument for legislation, though it gives no basis for a suit.
notes.41: Follow the four-step path from directive to right: a Part IV directive, courts read it into Article 21, an amendment adds Article 21A in 2002, and the RTE Act follows in 2009. The slide calls this interpretive move the most consequential doctrine for development work, since it explains most socio-economic rights case law.
notes.42: Expect conflict between social-justice laws and property or equality rights. The settled position is harmonious construction: the state may pursue Directive Principles while leaving the basic structure intact. The Ninth Schedule, created in 1951 to shield land-reform laws, is itself limited by the basic-structure doctrine.
notes.43: Part IV-A and Article 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, list citizens' duties. Ten were listed originally and an eleventh followed in 2002. The structural point is that duties address citizens, where Rights and Directive Principles address the state, and like Directive Principles they are unenforceable by themselves.
notes.44: Courts have used the environmental duty to support readings of Article 21, which is how a duty that cannot be enforced directly gains legal effect. Duties cannot be used to cut down a Fundamental Right; that argument has been made and has failed. Match each duty in the table to the value it echoes.
notes.45: Read the three parts together: rights protect the individual, Directive Principles direct the state, and duties remind citizens of their share. Check the table's last column, since only Part III is enforceable. Courts have resisted invoking duties to qualify rights, because a duty that cannot be enforced cannot cut down a right that can.
notes.47: India follows the parliamentary model: the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers come from the legislature and answer to it, and the President is head of state who acts on ministerial advice. A government that loses a Lok Sabha vote falls. Written supremacy and federalism distinguish the Indian version from Britain's.
notes.48: Learn the three organs and what checks each. The separation is functional, because the executive sits inside the legislature, so the check between them is political. That places most of the structural load on judicial review, which is why judicial independence is treated as part of the basic structure.
notes.49: Use the comparison table to learn the two Houses. The Lok Sabha is directly elected, can be dissolved and holds the government's confidence. The Rajya Sabha represents states, is permanent with one-third retiring every two years, and can only recommend on Money Bills. The Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is a live issue.
notes.50: The figures on this slide are approximate maxima and show no current strength: around 550 for the Lok Sabha and around 250 for the Rajya Sabha. The point is where power lies. The government is made and unmade in the larger directly elected House, so a majority there decides who governs.
notes.51: Distinguish power in law from power in practice. The President is the nominal executive who acts on advice, the Prime Minister leads the executive though the text says little about the office, and real power sits with the PM and Cabinet. The President keeps discretion in narrow cases such as a hung House.
notes.52: Follow a Bill through its stages and note where each can stop. Both Houses must agree on ordinary Bills, a joint sitting can resolve a deadlock, and the President may return a Bill once for reconsideration. Money Bills favour the Lok Sabha, and joint sittings are unavailable for Constitutional Amendment Bills.
notes.53: India does not copy the rigid American separation. The executive sits inside the legislature, and the independent judiciary is the keystone because judicial review can strike down both unconstitutional laws and unlawful executive action. Use the table to name who exercises each check, from questions in the Lok Sabha to basic structure.
notes.55: Federalism means sovereignty shared between the Union and the states. Use the table to find where each federal feature sits. The last row is the departure from the classical model: Parliament can redraw state boundaries by ordinary majority after hearing the state legislature, whose views are not binding. Hence holding-together federalism.
notes.56: The chart and table give approximate, illustrative counts of entries in the three lists: about a hundred Union, sixty State and fifty Concurrent. The trend is the lesson. Subjects have moved from the State List toward the Concurrent and Union Lists, with education and forests moved by the 42nd Amendment.
notes.57: Learn the three lists by example: Union (defence, currency, railways), State (police, public health, agriculture, land) and Concurrent (education, forests, criminal law). On the Concurrent List the Union law generally prevails in a clash. Residuary powers belong to Parliament under Article 248, another departure from classical federalism.
notes.58: Read the table as a checklist of centralising features: residuary powers (248), Union prevailing on concurrent subjects (254), President's Rule (356), a Centre-appointed Governor (155) and Parliament's power over boundaries (Article 3). Bommai (1994) made Article 356 reviewable, required a floor test, and held federalism part of the basic structure.
notes.59: The strong Centre was a deliberate choice, made in the shadow of Partition and the integration of princely states. The trade-off is that a Centre strong enough to hold the nation together can crowd the states. The correction came from the courts and coalition politics, and Bommai constrained Article 356 more than any amendment did.
notes.60: Much governance is cooperative, so a single programme often involves Union funds, state implementation and local delivery. Learn the four bodies: Finance Commission, GST Council, Inter-State Council and centrally sponsored schemes. For practitioners, most implementation questions are questions about the funding split and the conditions attached.
notes.61: Memorise the three emergency provisions with their Articles: national emergency (352), President's Rule (356) and financial emergency (360, never proclaimed). A national emergency has been proclaimed three times, most consequentially in 1975. The 44th Amendment tightened the trigger, the parliamentary approval requirement and the protection of Articles 20 and 21.
notes.62: Federalism in India is asymmetric. Scheduled Areas fall under the Fifth Schedule, tribal areas in the North East under the Sixth, certain states under Articles 371 onward and Union Territories under Article 239 onward. If you work in a Scheduled Area, the Fifth Schedule and PESA change what the Gram Sabha can decide.
notes.64: India has one integrated judiciary: the Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts in the states and subordinate courts below, applying both Union and state law. Remember that Article 226 reaches any legal right beyond Fundamental Rights, so the High Court is usually the practical first destination.
notes.65: Four safeguards protect independence: secure tenure, salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, limits on legislative discussion of judges' conduct and the collegium appointment process. The collegium is a judicial creation and absent from the text. The NJAC was struck down in 2015 as violating judicial independence, which is part of the basic structure.
notes.66: Judicial review is how supremacy is enforced: a statute that conflicts with the Constitution is void to that extent. Use the table's two columns to see what courts can do and what they cannot. The boundary is contested, and charges of judicial overreach usually concern the second row. Articles 13, 32 and 226 carry the power.
notes.67: Learn the four jurisdictions: original (Union-state disputes and Article 32 petitions), appellate, advisory under Article 143, and special leave under Article 136. Article 136 is discretionary and very wide and accounts for a large share of the docket. An advisory opinion is not binding, and the Court may decline to answer.
notes.68: PIL relaxed standing, form, procedure and remedy, so a third party can act for the marginalised and even a letter can become a petition. Continuing mandamus keeps a case open, as in the right-to-food litigation. Hold both readings: the tool widened access, and it is also criticised for overreach and hard-to-implement orders.
notes.69: The question was whether Parliament's power to amend is unlimited. It arose from land-reform laws that conflicted with property rights and ran for two decades. The 1973 resolution gave neither side what it had asked for: Parliament may amend, subject to a core the courts identify.
notes.70: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) is the pivot: Parliament can amend any provision but cannot destroy the basic structure. A 13-judge bench, the largest ever, decided it, by a narrow majority on the central question. In practice no temporary majority can amend away elections, judicial review, federalism or secularism.
notes.71: There is no closed list of basic-structure features, by design. Learn the recurring ones and the case that recognised them: Bommai for federalism and secularism, Minerva Mills for judicial review, and Indira Nehru Gandhi for free and fair elections. Case-by-case development gives flexibility, and critics call the doctrine judicially undefined.
notes.73: The third tier is local government. Compare the two columns: before 1992 local bodies existed at state discretion, and afterwards elections every five years, reserved seats and a State Finance Commission became constitutional requirements. Remember the gap the slide flags: the amendments mandate structure and leave devolution of power to the states.
notes.74: The 73rd Amendment added Part IX for panchayats and the 74th added Part IX-A for municipalities, both in force in 1993. Each added a Schedule listing subjects states may devolve. The word may carries the weight, since the Schedules are lists of possible subjects and make no mandatory transfer.
notes.75: This slide pictures the three panchayat levels: Gram Panchayat at village level, Panchayat Samiti at block level and Zila Parishad at district level. Each is elected with its own powers, mirroring the federal idea of nested levels. Smaller states may have fewer tiers, so check your own state.
notes.76: The Gram Sabha is the assembly of all adult voters and the only face-to-face democratic body in the constitutional scheme. The table pairs what it may do with what often happens: plans ratified, lists endorsed, quorum missed. The slide's fixes are concrete: advance notice, convenient timing, a circulated agenda, minutes read aloud and enforced quorum.
notes.77: The amendments reserve seats for SC and ST in proportion to population and for women, including chairperson offices by rotation. The constitutional floor for women is one-third, and many states raised it to one-half by state law. Hold the achievement and the caveat: a major shift in who holds power, alongside proxy leadership.
notes.78: Remember the three Fs: functions, funds and functionaries. Law lists 29 functions in the Eleventh Schedule, yet transfer is partial, funds are often tied and small, and staff usually report to departments. The third row is the binding constraint. Check your state's devolution position before advising a community on what the panchayat can decide.
notes.79: PESA extends Panchayati Raj to Fifth Schedule areas with stronger Gram Sabha powers: a say over land acquisition, control of minor forest produce, a role in minor mineral leases and recognition of customary practice. The slide pairs it with the Forest Rights Act 2006 as the most powerful instrument for community control of resources.
notes.81: The drafters wanted a middle path between a constitution too rigid to adapt and one so flexible that a majority rewrites it at will. Their answer was special majorities, several amendment routes of differing difficulty, and a protected core. Notice that the protected core came later, from the courts in Kesavananda.
notes.82: Article 368 is the Constitution's clause for revising itself, covering Parliament's power and procedure, the special majorities, and for some provisions the consent of the states. The line to hold is the limit: since 1973 it cannot be used to destroy the basic structure.
notes.83: Learn the three routes as a ladder: simple majority outside Article 368, special majority, and special majority plus ratification by half the state legislatures for federal provisions. The deeper the change, the higher the bar. The final note matters: ratification needs only half the states, a weaker protection than in some federations.
notes.84: The chart is illustrative and shows a pattern only: the Constitution has been amended over a hundred times, and the 1970s stand out. That decade combined land reform, the Emergency and the basic-structure battle. Use it as a reminder of when pressure on the text peaked, and take no exact counts from it.
notes.85: Learn the 42nd and 44th as a pair: one made during the Emergency, the other undoing much of it. Then place the others: 1st (Ninth Schedule), 73rd and 74th (local government), 86th (Article 21A) and 101st (GST). The 44th also took the right to property out of Part III and put it in Article 300A.
notes.86: Follow the four steps as a sequence of moves between Parliament and courts: Golaknath limits amending of rights, Parliament asserts its power through the 24th and 25th Amendments, Kesavananda allows amendment but forbids destroying the basic structure, and Minerva Mills holds limited amending power part of that structure. Neither side has the last word alone.
notes.87: The unamendable core protects democracy from its own winners. A temporary majority, however large, cannot abolish elections, remove judicial review, end federalism or repeal secularism. The doctrine is counter-majoritarian by design, which is both the objection to it and the defence: democracy needs rules a majority cannot change.
notes.88: The Constitution changes in two ways: formal amendment, which is visible and numbered, and interpretation, which leaves no trace in the text. The slide argues the second has changed daily life more. Hence reading the bare Article is insufficient: what Article 21 means today is found in the cases.
notes.89: The framework has held through the Emergency, a century of amendments, shifting politics and rapid social change, which is the strongest empirical argument for its design. The closing note adds a condition: it is never self-executing. Its endurance depends on people defending institutions, which is what constitutionalism means.
notes.91: Separate having a constitution from constitutionalism. Many states have excellent texts and no constitutionalism. The table gives four observable tests: restraints observed, rights enforceable in practice, independent courts and free and fair elections. Check them by asking who was appointed, what happened to the last inconvenient judgment and who counted the votes.
notes.92: Compare the charity and rights framings row by row. A rights-holder is owed accountability, exclusion is a violation, and there is a grievance route and a court. The framing changes what a programme builds, and it places the duty on the state, which the programme supports and never replaces.
notes.93: Each landmark welfare law has a constitutional root: RTE in Article 21A, RTI in Article 19(1)(a), MGNREGA in the right to livelihood under Article 21, the Forest Rights Act in Articles 21 and 46, and the SC/ST Atrocities Act in Articles 15 and 17. The root stays available even if the statute's own remedy is blocked.
notes.94: RTI converts an informal request into a legal obligation with a deadline, generally thirty days. Ask for a specific file in place of an opinion, because a question can be refused while a document request usually cannot. Remember the appeal path: first appeal, then the Information Commission. Fees are waived below the poverty line.
notes.95: Puttaswamy (2017) held privacy a fundamental right under Article 21, by a nine-judge bench. It is the vivid example of the living Constitution, since the word appears nowhere in the text. Its test of legality, necessity and proportionality now governs restrictions on rights and sits beneath the DPDP Act obligations on handling data.
notes.96: NALSA (2014) recognised transgender persons as a third gender with a right to self-identify, and Navtej Johar (2018) read down Section 377 to decriminalise consensual same-sex relations. Both rest on dignity and equality under Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21. The Transgender Persons Act 2019 followed NALSA and is criticised on several points.
notes.97: Use the table to attach an Article to ordinary acts: voting (326), filing an RTI (19(1)(a)), approaching a court (32 and 226), a Gram Sabha holding its panchayat to account (Part IX), forming a union (19(1)(c)). Naming the basis converts a request into a claim, and rights literacy transfers to the people you work with.
notes.98: Start with the bare text, especially the Preamble and Part III, which the slide says run to around twenty pages and give the highest return. Add Basu as a working reference, Austin for how and why the Constitution was made, and the Debates for what a provision meant. Ambedkar's closing speech is the argument the document rests on.
notes.99: These five takeaways each carry a practical consequence for how you handle a denied entitlement. If you keep only one, keep the third: power is divided, so ask which level owes the duty. Most implementation disputes turn on that question, and the answer is usually in the Seventh Schedule.
